critique.good: Neighborhoods, prices and floor descriptions stay on one line, making the identifying and numeric fields easy to scan. Headers are clear.
critique.problems: The notes form narrow, dense blocks, making every row unusually tall and leaving large empty areas in the other columns. The floor column is generously sized for short entries.
critique.cause: The 143px floor column preserves complete floor descriptions at the expense of the 174px notes column, which forces notes to wrap to as many as seven lines.

critique.good: Neighborhoods and prices remain intact, while the wider notes column gives the table a more balanced rhythm than r0A. Floor information remains readable over two lines.
critique.problems: Notes still drive tall rows, and the floor descriptions break at inconsistent points: in some rows the elevator phrase is split between lines.
critique.cause: The 217px notes column remains relatively narrow, while the 100px floor column is too narrow to keep every elevator phrase together with the preceding floor text.

critique.good: The 270px notes column produces shorter, more even rows and gives the descriptive content room to breathe. Floor and elevator information is consistently readable on two lines.
critique.problems: Two multiword neighborhood names wrap, weakening the row identifiers. Every monthly price also wraps, adding repeated second lines to the comparison fields.
critique.cause: The 85px neighborhood column provides only 64px of text width, below the 76px needed for the longest name. The 85px price column similarly falls short of the 90px needed for the full price and monthly qualifier.

critique.good: Neighborhoods and room counts scan cleanly, and the notes have the most breathing room of the three designs. Prices and floor information wrap consistently into two lines.
critique.problems: The monthly price qualifier creates a second line in every price cell. The long notes still dominate row height, leaving substantial empty space in the other columns.
critique.cause: The 85px price column is too narrow for the complete price phrase; the 258px notes column must accommodate much longer text than any other column.

critique.good: Complete prices sit on one line, making the primary numeric comparison especially easy. Neighborhoods remain intact, and floor information wraps consistently.
critique.problems: The notes feel denser and have shorter, more fragmented lines than in r1A, without reducing overall table height.
critique.cause: The 111px price column takes 26px from the notes, leaving them 232px wide.

critique.good: The notes retain reasonable width, and neighborhoods, room counts and price amounts remain easy to scan.
critique.problems: The fifth floor cell breaks the elevator phrase across lines, unlike the other floor cells. Prices still wrap, so the extra floor width does not improve the overall rhythm.
critique.cause: At 93px, the floor column is wide enough to fit the first word of the elevator phrase on the first line but too narrow to keep the whole phrase there; the price column remains 85px.

critique.good: The neighborhood names stay on one line, making the shaded row headers easy to scan. Prices remain intact, floor and elevator information form two clear lines, and the notes have enough width for natural wrapping.
critique.problems: Every monthly qualifier wraps below its price, giving the price column a repeated two-line pattern. The notes still produce dense four- and five-line blocks.
critique.cause: At 101px, the price column provides 80px of content width, less than the 90px needed for the full price expression. The 242px notes column must accommodate substantially longer text.

critique.good: The wider notes column gives the descriptions a more relaxed measure, while prices and floor expressions remain readable. The numeric columns are compact and easy to compare.
critique.problems: The final neighborhood name wraps onto two lines, weakening the consistent scan of the row headers. Prices also use two lines, and the wider notes do not reduce the overall table height.
critique.cause: The 90px neighborhood column leaves 69px for content, less than the 76px needed for the longest name. The 85px price column is too narrow for the monthly qualifier to stay on the first line.

critique.good: Neighborhood names and complete monthly prices stay on one line, making the main comparison fields especially easy to scan. The notes remain readable and no words split.
critique.problems: Several floor cells break the elevator description across two lines, so the absence of an elevator takes three lines in total. The narrower notes column also produces denser wrapping.
critique.cause: The 79px floor column leaves only 58px for content, too little to keep the short elevator phrase together. The 111px price column takes space from both floor and notes.

understanding.purpose: Compare rental apartments in Tel Aviv by neighborhood, monthly price, size, floor and descriptive notes.
understanding.reading: Readers scan the neighborhood names to identify listings, compare the numeric attributes across rows, then read the notes for details and tradeoffs.
groups: Neighborhood identifies each listing; price and rooms are the primary comparison fields.
Floor and elevator availability describe accessibility; the floor cell combines both.
Notes contain longer qualitative details and benefit most from flexible width.
keep_intact: Neighborhood names where possible, especially multiword names.
Prices and their currency symbols; room counts and decimal values.
Floor numbers and short floor expressions.
may_wrap: Long notes can wrap naturally between words.
Elevator descriptions can wrap after the floor information.
The monthly price qualifier can wrap if necessary; note wrapping may already set the row height.

bad.why: The narrow neighborhood, price and floor columns would force frequent wrapping of the identifying and comparison fields, while giving the notes disproportionate space.

contrast.why: The narrow neighborhood, price and floor columns would force frequent wrapping of the identifying and comparison fields, while giving the notes disproportionate space.

final.rationale: r1B and r3A are identical: they keep neighborhood names and monthly prices on one line, making the principal comparisons easy to scan from right to left. Floor and elevator information fits in two lines, while the wider notes column carries the longer prose without breaking words. The notes determine row height, so the extra width given to prices does not make the table taller.

general: Give identifying fields and frequently compared values enough width to remain easy to scan.
Allocate width according to content and reading purpose, not equal proportions or table height alone.
specific: A 111px price column keeps the amount and monthly unit together; 85–101px separates them.
The 58px rooms column fits its content, leaving more room for floor details and notes.

final.tradeoffs: A wider notes column produces more relaxed prose, as in r1A, but places the monthly unit on a separate line. r2B gives notes still more room at the cost of wrapping one neighborhood name; r2C preserves single-line prices but wraps some floor details onto three lines.
final.uncertain: The ranges are conservative estimates, not independently rendered tests. Small width changes can alter individual Hebrew line breaks, and designers may reasonably prefer more space for notes over keeping each price on one line.

A.why: Neighborhoods and prices stay on one line, room counts scan easily, and floor details wrap into coherent phrases. Notes have enough width for readable lines.

B.why: Neighborhoods remain intact and the notes read comfortably, but every price separates its monthly unit onto a second line.

C.why: The notes have reasonable line lengths and neighborhoods remain intact, but prices wrap throughout and one floor entry splits the elevator phrase.

D.why: Wide notes are easy to read, but narrow neighborhood and floor columns fragment identifiers and floor details; one neighborhood even breaks within a word.

E.why: Notes have useful space, but neighborhood names wrap and some prices separate the currency symbol from the amount. Floor details also break into short fragments.

F.why: The notes are squeezed into a narrow strip, producing very tall rows and making each apartment difficult to scan as a unit. The room-count column has excessive empty space.

reviews.unsure: B and C are close: their notes have slightly different line breaks, but both make the same recurring compromise in the price column.

A.why: Neighborhood names stay intact, and the notes have a readable measure. Prices wrap consistently onto two lines, though one floor entry breaks less cleanly than the others.

B.why: The wide notes column reads comfortably, but neighborhood names wrap and some prices split the currency symbol onto its own line, weakening comparison.

C.why: Neighborhood names and complete prices stay on one line, room counts are easy to scan, and floor details wrap consistently. Notes remain readable despite their narrower column.

D.why: The narrow neighborhood column breaks a name within a word, while floor details fragment across several lines. The extra space given to notes comes at the expense of identifying and comparing apartments.

E.why: The notes column is so narrow that prose breaks into a long stack of short lines, creating very tall rows and large empty areas in the other columns.

F.why: Neighborhood names stay intact, floor details wrap consistently, and the notes have a comfortable measure. Prices still require two lines, making them slightly less immediate to scan.

reviews.unsure: C trades some notes-column width for single-line prices; a reader prioritizing the descriptive notes might prefer F.
